chunks: Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār narrated from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام that he said:
"The maḥṣūr is other than the maṣdūd."

And he said: "The maḥṣūr is the sick person, and the maṣdūd is the one whom the polytheists turn back, just as they turned back the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم and his companions, not because of illness. The maṣdūd, women become lawful for him, while the maḥṣūr, women do not become lawful for him."

key_terms.النِّسَاءُ: Women; mentioned here regarding the legal consequence tied to each category.
key_terms.الْمَحْصُورُ: A pilgrim prevented from completing the rites due to illness.
key_terms.الْمَرِيضُ: The sick person; here, the defining case of al-maḥṣūr.
key_terms.الْمَصْدُودُ: A pilgrim obstructed or turned back by external force, such as enemies.
key_terms.الْمُشْرِكُونَ: The polytheists who prevent the pilgrim from proceeding.
key_terms.رَسُولَ اللَّهِ: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, cited here as a historical example.

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between al-maḥṣūr and al-maṣdūd in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith distinguishes between two legal categories in hajj or ʿumrah: the maḥṣūr, who is prevented by illness, and the maṣdūd, who is blocked by external enemies. It explains that the rulings differ between them, including the legal status of relations with women after being prevented from completing the rites. The report also recalls the historical case of the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم being turned back by the polytheists.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: Hadith.3104 - Muawiyah ibn Ammar narrated from Abu Abdullah (as) that he said:
"The Mahsur (prevented) is not the same as the Masdood (barred)."

Imam (as) further said: "Mahsur refers to the sick person, while Masdood refers to one who is prevented by the polytheists, as they prevented the Messenger of Allah (swt) (peace and blessings be upon him and his family) and his companions, not due to illness. The Masdood is permitted to engage with women, but the Mahsur is not permitted to engage with women."
